section_summary: This section documents the Japanese internal political crisis of June through September 1934, marked by the collapse of the Saito Cabinet and the appointment and installation of Admiral Keisuke Okada as Prime Minister. Embassy despatches from Tokyo and internal State Department memoranda analyze Okada's ministerial appointments as a moderate compromise designed to preserve national stability, counterbalance reactionary militarists, and prepare for upcoming naval disarmament negotiations. Additional documents cover party politics and internal fractures within the Seiyukai, Japanese military intentions and Mongol administration in Manchuria, the Okada administration's formal ten-point statement of policy, and constitutional procedures regarding Diet dissolution and military budget approvals.

subfiles.about: Concluding page of a despatch analyzing political difficulties facing the Saito Cabinet and prospects of General Ugaki becoming Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Concluding page of Despatch No. 814 on Ugaki's chances of succeeding Saito: military opposes him over disarmament, and the Seiyukai is divided.
subfiles.title: Political Difficulties Besetting the Saito Cabinet and Candidates for the Premiership (Despatch No. 814)

subfiles.about: Reports growing indications that the Saito Cabinet will be forced to resign and may be reconstituted.
subfiles.summary: Grew cables strong indications the Saito Cabinet will resign en bloc and probably be reconstituted under Saito, as no consensus successor exists.
subfiles.title: Impending Resignation and Possible Reconstitution of the Saito Cabinet (Telegram No. 136)

subfiles.about: Announces the en bloc resignation of the Saito Cabinet on July 3, 1934.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Saito Cabinet resigned en bloc on July 3, 1934; a new cabinet is not expected for several days.
subfiles.title: Resignation En Bloc of the Saito Cabinet (Telegram No. 141)

subfiles.about: Comments on Tokyo Despatch No. 831, cautioning against overestimating the trend toward liberalism in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck agrees with Hamilton that Despatch No. 831 overstates Japan's liberal trend; progress will be slow, and rapid gains might provoke aggressive young officers.
subfiles.title: Trend Toward Liberalism in Japan

subfiles.about: Comments on Tokyo Despatch No. 831, addressing divided cabinet responsibility and corporate ties to political parties.
subfiles.summary: Dooman on Despatch No. 831: Saionji quietly places liberals, divided cabinet responsibility has precedent, and Mitsui and Mitsubishi fund both major parties.
subfiles.title: Comments on Tokyo Despatch No. 831 Concerning the Internal Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on the internal political situation in Japan, the appointment of Baron Ikki, and the balance between liberal and reactionary forces.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details an apparent swing toward liberalism and parliamentarism following Prince Saionji and Count Makino's appointment of Baron Dr. Ikki as President of the Privy Council over the reactionary Baron Hiranuma. The despatch examines the collapse of General Ugaki's bid for the Premiership due to military opposition, analyzes alternative candidates including Count Kiyoura, Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki, and General Araki, and evaluates the financial scandal confronting Finance Minister Takahashi. It concludes with a comprehensive tabular lineup of liberal and reactionary influences in Japanese politics, business, and journalism.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Situation in Japan (Despatch No. 831)

subfiles.about: Reports that Admiral Keisuke Okada has been charged by the Emperor with forming a new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Admiral Keisuke Okada received the Imperial command to form a cabinet after Saito's fall; members not yet announced.
subfiles.title: Imperial Command to Admiral Okada to Form New Cabinet (Telegram No. 144)

subfiles.about: Analyzes the causes behind the Saito Cabinet's fall, the selection of Admiral Okada as Premier, and naval limitation policy.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Eugene H. Dooman
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck submits to Under Secretary Phillips and Secretary Hull an analytical memorandum prepared by Eugene H. Dooman regarding the selection of Admiral Keisuke Okada as Prime Minister. Dooman argues that the Saito Cabinet resigned due to budgetary conflicts over military and naval estimates rather than subordinate corruption scandals. He assesses Okada's appointment as a moderate compromise designed to manage upcoming naval disarmament negotiations effectively. Attached to the memorandum are a historical table of Japanese cabinets since 1918 and a 1932 Herald Tribune interview with Okada concerning naval policy.
subfiles.title: Selection of Admiral Keisuke Okada to Form a New Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports confirmed appointments to the new Okada Cabinet and cites Okada's 1932 interview on naval policy.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Hirota, Hayashi and Osumi keep their posts and Fujii becomes Finance Minister. He cites Fleisher's 1932 interview with Okada as key to the premier's outlook.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Appointments and Reference to Okada's 1932 Interview (Telegram No. 146)

subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential assessment by a high-ranking Japanese informant regarding the moderate composition of the Okada Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays an informant calling the Okada Cabinet a victory for moderates and good for US-Japan relations; Osumi may be replaced by Nomura or Kobayashi. Grew sees a trend away from aggressive nationalism.
subfiles.title: Confidential Assessment of the New Okada Cabinet (Telegram No. 147)

subfiles.about: Notes Wilfrid Fleisher's analysis of the stiffer naval policy expected under the Okada-Osumi combination.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck cites Fleisher: Okada is not an extreme big-navy man, but the Okada-Osumi team will pursue a firmer naval policy than Saito.
subfiles.title: Wilfrid Fleisher's Comments on Japanese Naval Policy Under Okada Cabinet

subfiles.about: Provides biographical background on Admirals Kichisaburo Nomura and Seizo Kobayashi as rumored successors to Navy Minister Osumi.
subfiles.summary: Dooman profiles Admiral Nomura, a pro-American former Washington attaché, and Kobayashi, who defended the London Treaty and was later demoted.
subfiles.title: Biographical Information on Admirals Nomura and Kobayashi

subfiles.about: Reports on the Seiyukai party's threatened boycott of the Okada Cabinet over ministerial portfolio allocations.
subfiles.summary: Fleisher reports Premier Okada's cabinet formation is hampered by a threatened Seiyukai boycott; Mochizuki and Tokonami declined posts, and Okada sought mediation with party president Suzuki.
subfiles.title: Majority Party Boycott Faces Japan's Cabinet

subfiles.about: Announces the successful completion and formal installation of the Okada Cabinet before the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Okada completed his Cabinet, formally installed on July 8, 1934; a full report follows by mail.
subfiles.title: Completion and Formal Installation of the Okada Cabinet (Telegram No. 153)

subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum of conversation with journalist A. T. Steele regarding Japanese military policy, Mongols, and migration in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Minister Nelson Trusler Johnson transmits a memorandum of conversation with journalist A. T. Steele, who recently completed a tour of Manchuria. Steele reported that Japanese officials, including Major-General Okamura, claimed there would be no military advance into North China while strategic construction remains unfinished. Steele also detailed administrative and religious reforms among the Mongols supervised by Lieutenant-General Yoda, as well as the difficulties and local opposition facing armed Japanese agricultural immigrants along the lower Sungari River.
subfiles.title: The Attitude of Japanese Officials in Manchuria Toward War, Mongols, and Migration of Japanese (Despatch No. 2796)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing a report from Grew regarding rumors of Admiral Suetsugu joining the new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 883 (July 5, 1934): new cabinet not yet announced; Admiral Suetsugu's name frequently mentioned.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet Concerning New Cabinet and Admiral Suetsugu (File No. 894.00/532)

subfiles.about: Reviews and commends Tokyo Despatch No. 896 on the formation of the Okada Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Memo calls Despatch No. 896 interesting and readable, wanting more on Saito's resignation but recommending the section on why Okada was appointed.
subfiles.title: Comments on Tokyo Despatch No. 896 Regarding the Okada Cabinet

subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive report on the formation, membership, factional politics, and policies of the Okada Cabinet, with biographic data.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew presents an extensive analysis of the newly installed Cabinet of Admiral Keisuke Okada, detailing the political background of Okada's selection as a compromise mediator between liberal and military factions. He explains the breakdown of party negotiations, resulting in the expulsion of three Seiyukai members who accepted cabinet posts and the Minseito's cooperation. Individual ministerial statements on foreign relations, national defense, and financial policy are analyzed, accompanied by eight confidential biographic data sheets for the newly appointed ministers.
subfiles.title: The Okada Cabinet (Despatch No. 896)

subfiles.about: Analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 918 and evaluates the Okada Cabinet's statement of policy and Diet dissolution prospects.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reviews Despatch No. 918, calling the Okada Cabinet's policy declaration vague, and thinks the government unlikely to dissolve the Diet against Seiyukai opposition.
subfiles.title: Review of Tokyo Despatch No. 918 on the Okada Cabinet's Statement of Policy
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Transmits the formal ten-point statement of policy issued by the Okada Cabinet on July 20, 1934.
subfiles.summary: Grew sends the English text of the Okada Cabinet's ten-point policy statement, covering administrative purification, defense, finance and relief. He notes criticism of it as vague on agricultural relief.
subfiles.title: Statement of Policy by Okada Cabinet (Despatch No. 918)

subfiles.about: Reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 908 and analyzes constitutional issues surrounding military estimates and Diet dissolution.
subfiles.summary: Dooman on Despatch No. 908: the Army and Navy fear a Seiyukai veto of the 1935 budget; the Seiyukai will probably avoid forcing dissolution.
subfiles.title: Review and Comment on Tokyo Despatch No. 908 Regarding Japanese Political Parties
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Analyzes the resurgence of political party influence and factional strife within the Seiyukai under the Okada administration.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports political parties regaining standing and a trend back toward party government under Okada, with militarist influence declining. Details Seiyukai splits under Suzuki and its hostility to the cabinet.
subfiles.title: Present Position of Political Parties in Japan (Despatch No. 908)
